bullets: Quasar links proposed API changes to actual consumer references, giving producers concrete evidence for release decisions.
It highlights the challenge of assessing downstream impact when a library change originates in one repo but affects many others.
The tool aids both producers and coding agents by revealing which consumers still rely on changed symbols, informing migration strategies.
Quasar links a library’s API change to actual usage in other projects, showing how many consumers still rely on the altered code.
This visibility helps producers decide whether to remove or keep a deprecated method, by revealing its “blast radius” – the spread of affected projects.
The tool also informs automated coding agents, giving them cross‑repository context to assess downstream risk and plan safe migrations.
Quasar links proposed API changes to observed consumer references across Netflix's shared Java libraries, giving producers concrete evidence of downstream impact.
The tool tracks API diffs, identifies remaining calls to deprecated methods, and maps consumer versions, enabling producers to assess risk before removal.
By exposing blast radius, Quasar supports automated agents in planning migrations and testing, reducing manual effort in large, independently evolving repository ecosystems.

articles.title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes

bullets: Introduces SpecEvo, a multi-LLM framework that uses lightweight models for parallel speculation and an Advisor to consolidate evidence, reserving expensive frontier models for strategic interventions.
The workflow alternates speculative generation and evidence consolidation, enabling cost‑efficient exploration while maintaining high performance across 176 scientific and algorithmic tasks.
SpecEvo reduces API cost by up to 80%, improves evaluation efficiency 1.5× on equation discovery, and outperforms CO‑Bench baselines by 3.8%.
SpecEvo uses many small LLMs (Speculators) to generate and tweak program ideas, while a lightweight Advisor learns from successes and failures to guide future searches.
A powerful frontier LLM (Navigator) checks the population at checkpoints, making big changes like combining ideas, fine‑tuning, or re‑framing when progress stalls.
Across 176 tasks, SpecEvo cuts API costs by up to 80%, speeds up evaluations 1.5×, and outperforms strong baselines, showing cost‑efficient scientific discovery.
SpecEvo: multi-LLM framework using lightweight Speculators and Advisor for candidate generation and evidence consolidation, with frontier Navigator for strategic interventions.
Workflow: speculate-then-consolidate delegates routine exploration to inexpensive models, reserving frontier reasoning for sparse checkpoints, reducing API cost up to 80%.
Performance: on 176 tasks across four domains, matches/outperforms frontier baselines, 1.5× evaluation efficiency on equation discovery, 3.8% improvement over CO-Bench.

articles.title: SpecEvo: Speculative Evolution with Large Language Models for Cost-Efficient Scientific Discovery

bullets: Introduces First Passage Attention (FPA) as a new attention mechanism that replaces path summation with path extrema to selectively erase intermediate context.
FPA generalizes Forgetting Transformer, forming a stack of alive keys via a shared learned walk, enabling constant-dimension heads to realize any subset of keys.
Experiments show one-layer FPA outperforms softmax and FoX baselines, matching FoX perplexity and achieving perfect passkey retrieval at 8× training length with compressed cache.
First Passage Attention (FPA) replaces cumulative decay in attention with a path‑extrema rule that can selectively erase intermediate tokens while keeping older ones.
FPA generalizes the Forgetting Transformer; its constant‑size head can keep any chosen keys, unlike softmax heads that need size proportional to key count.
In tests, a single‑layer FPA matches FoX (forgetting transformer) on perplexity and retrieves passkeys 8× longer than training, even with a 25% compressed cache.
FPA replaces softmax path summation with path extrema, lowering a key’s logit by the deepest dip of a learned scalar field over the span.
Shared learned walk makes alive keys stack; a constant‑dimension head can realize any subset, whereas softmax heads require linear size.
Synthetic tests show one‑layer FPA converges to target key sets; 110M model matches FoX perplexity and retrieves 8× longer passkeys with 25% cache compression.

articles.title: First Passage Attention

bullets: HiddenLens is a six-layer BERT-LLM pipeline that detects, classifies, questions, and resolves hidden assumptions in natural-language software requirements.
The framework localizes unresolved spans, articulates assumptions with risk, classifies them into six NFR categories, and generates ranked clarification options.
A new HiddenLens Corpus contains 312 requirements annotated with 847 hidden assumptions, supporting training and evaluation of the framework.
HiddenLens is a six-layer BERT-LLM pipeline that finds hidden assumptions in software requirements, not just vague language.
Layers 1–6 locate unclear spans, explain assumptions, classify into six non‑functional categories, suggest clarifications, let humans edit, then rewrite explicit, testable requirements.
HiddenLens Corpus contains 312 requirements with 847 annotated hidden assumptions across performance, security, scalability, usability, reliability, and domain, aiding future research.

articles.title: HiddenLens: A Multi-Layer LLM Framework for Detecting and Resolving Hidden Assumptions in Software Requirements

bullets: PerMIT protects LLM agents by enforcing explicit trust on user inputs and gate-confirmed values, mediating untrusted environment data via a finite memory interface.
Two machine-checked integrity theorems in Lean 4 guarantee that only gate‑approved memory can influence sensitive actions, reducing attacks to a single auditable decision.
Community endorsements accumulate, and simulations show that as the community grows, poisoning risks drop while per‑user verification effort stays low.
PerMIT is a memory architecture that protects persistent memory from injection attacks by only trusting user inputs and values confirmed at a gate.
It uses a finite memory interface and two machine‑checked integrity theorems (Lean 4) to ensure environment data reaches sensitive actions only after gate confirmation.
Community endorsements accumulate; once enough users confirm, items become community‑confirmed, reducing verification effort while lowering poisoning and false‑eviction risks.
PerMIT enforces integrity of persistent memory by trusting only user-typed inputs confirmed at a gate, mediating untrusted values via a finite interface.
Two machine‑checked (Lean 4) integrity theorems guarantee that environment‑derived data reaches sensitive actions only after gate confirmation and influences agents solely through gate display.
Community endorsements log exact content; once sufficiently endorsed, items become community‑confirmed, reducing per‑user verification effort and lowering poisoning risk as the community scales.

articles.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust

bullets: Handshake: initial exchange where agents find each other, learn abilities, and set up a session; measured across three protocols (MCP, A2A, ACP).
Round‑trip count dominates cost: legacy MCP needs 3 round trips (~230 ms at 50 ms RTT), A2A only 1 (~61 ms).
Handshake also scales with capability inventory: each capability costs 24–107 tokens; a 200‑capability agent uses 11% of a 200k‑token context before reading its own task.

articles.title: The Cost of Saying Hello: An Empirical Study of Handshake Overhead in AI Agent Communication Protocols

bullets: Gandalf reduces KV cache writes by prioritizing full-attention data for SSD offloading, extending SSD lifetime without lowering cache hit rate.
The system uses historical access patterns and attention type to decide which KV cache entries to write to SSD.
Evaluation shows Gandalf extends SSD lifetime by 7.3× on average, maintaining negligible impact on LLM serving cost.
KV caching speeds LLM serving but uses too much memory; SSDs expand capacity, yet heavy writes shrink SSD life from years to months.
Traditional gating of writes based on past access patterns hurts cache hit rate because different attention types share patterns but need different future data.
Gandalf prioritizes full-attention KV cache writes to SSD, extending lifetime 7.3× while keeping hit rate unchanged; it uses attention type info to guide writes.
Gandalf offloads KV cache to SSD, prioritizing full‑attention entries over others to reduce write amplification while preserving hit rates.
Uses access‑pattern gating combined with attention‑type awareness to limit SSD writes, extending lifetime by ~7.3× without cost increase.
Evaluation shows negligible hit‑rate drop, achieving 7.3X SSD longevity gain in multi‑round LLM serving workloads.

articles.title: Gandalf: Flash Shall Not Die! Increasing Flash Storage Lifetime for KV Cache Offloading in LLM Serving

bullets: Introduces VeriEvolve, an evaluator-first evolution framework that builds an executable evaluator before optimizing agents for realistic stateful tasks.
Synthesizes instruction-grounded challenge states and freezes the evaluator as fitness signal, then refines it using counterfactual test cases from strong/weak runs.
Applied to 30 MCPMark filesystem tasks, it raises success rates for GLM‑5.2 and Claude, proving evaluators guide search when observability and verification exist.
VeriEvolve builds an evaluator first, creating test states from instructions and a program that checks them, giving agents a clear success signal.
In 30 tasks, it built 30 evaluators, 141 states, raising agent success from 6/30 to 18/30 for one model and 27/30 to 30/30 for another.
Tests on PostgreSQL, Playwright, Notion, GitHub show limits in observing results, state representation, and search, proving evaluators help when success can be seen.
VeriEvolve constructs evaluator‑first evolution, synthesizing instruction‑grounded challenge states and an executable evaluator that serves as a frozen fitness signal during each workflow round.
Between rounds, the evaluator is revised by converting strong and weak run end states into counterfactual test pairs, refining 30 evaluators across 30 MCPMark tasks.

Results: 141/141 agreement on generated suites, 113/122 on held‑out states, raising GLM‑5.2 success 6/30→18/30 and Claude 27/30→30/30; cross‑environment tests on PostgreSQL, Playwright, Notion, GitHub.

articles.title: VeriEvolve: Evaluator-First Evolution for Tool-Using Agents

bullets: LLMSeg is a training-free pipeline that turns a vision-capable LLM into a text-prompted image segmenter without extra segmentation heads or training.
It uses three LLM-driven stages: detection and coarse description, B-spline tracing within bounding boxes, and iterative refinement with focus boxes until mask stabilizes.

Evaluated on ten referring and reasoning segmentation splits, open-vocabulary instance and semantic segmentation, and zero-shot detection, it matches or surpasses specialist SAM models using Gemini-3.7-Flash.
LLMSeg is a training‑free pipeline that turns a multimodal large language model into a text‑prompted image segmenter, eliminating extra segmentation heads.
It performs segmentation in three LLM‑driven stages: detect instances, trace boundaries with closed B‑splines, and iteratively refine until masks stabilize.
Across ten referring and reasoning splits, plus open‑vocabulary datasets, LLMSeg matches or surpasses the specialist SAM model using only a Gemini‑3.7‑Flash backend.
LLMSeg is a training‑free, text‑prompted segmentation pipeline that uses a vision‑capable LLM (Gemini‑3.7‑Flash) to detect, describe, and segment instances via B‑splines.
It runs three stages: detect & describe instances; trace each with periodic B‑splines inside boxes; refine via focus boxes until mask stabilizes or budget ends.
Evaluate on ten ReasonSeg/RefCOCO splits, LVIS, COCO, SA‑Co, zero‑shot detection; matches or surpasses SAM 3 on identical instances.

articles.title: LLMSeg: Training-Free Text-Prompted Image Segmentation with B-Splines

bullets: Kernel-managed shared memory lets agents tag structured memories; the kernel handles retrieval, privacy, and prompt injection.
Evaluation on AIOS with GPT‑4o, Llama‑3.1, Qwen‑2.5 shows 2.4‑4.0 point personalization gains over unmanaged Mem0, significant at p < 10⁻¹⁸.
Compared to full context concatenation, kernel‑managed injection matches performance on two models, reduces prompt length, latency 15‑61% lower, and cuts token usage.
Kernel‑managed shared memory lets agents tag memories; the kernel retrieves, enforces privacy, and injects prompts, acting as the system’s core controller.
On AIOS, we tested GPT‑4o, Llama‑3.1, and Qwen‑2.5 across 1,800 trials, gaining 2.4–4.0 points over unmanaged memory (p < 10⁻¹⁸).
Compared to full context concatenation, kernel‑managed injection matches two models, slightly lags one, yet uses 15–61% fewer tokens, lower latency, and cheaper inference.
Introduces kernel-managed shared memory: agents write structured, tagged memories; kernel handles retrieval, privacy, prompt injection.
Implemented on AIOS; evaluated against Mem0, standard retrieval-augmented injection, and full context concatenation across GPT-4o, Llama-3.1:8B, Qwen-2.5:7B, 1,800 trials.
Kernel-managed approach improves personalization 2.4-4.0 points, matches or exceeds other methods, reduces latency 15-61%, lowers token usage and cost.

articles.title: Kernel-Managed Shared Memory for System-Wide Personalization

bullets: Introduces spiking ternary GRU (stGRU) combining ternary-weight gated recurrent unit for filtering and resonate-and-fire neurons for binary spike output.
Enables end‑to‑end training on LibriSpeech, achieving single‑digit WER (6.44% on test‑clean) without dense MACs or external language model.
Also attains 10.88% CER on Aishell‑1, demonstrating effectiveness on Mandarin speech and depth‑graded hierarchical representations.
Introduces spiking ternary GRU (stGRU) that separates filtering and integration, using ternary weights and resonate‑and‑fire neurons for efficient, event‑driven speech processing.
Trained end‑to‑end on LibriSpeech, stGRU models reach 6.44% WER on test‑clean without language models, the first spiking network to hit single‑digit error without dense MACs.
Also achieves 10.88% character error on Aishell‑1, showing the architecture works on Mandarin speech and builds a depth‑graded hierarchy of representations.
stGRU combines ternary-weight GRU temporal filtering with downstream Resonate‑and‑Fire neurons that emit binary spikes, eliminating LIF decay and enabling native event‑based training.
End‑to‑end training on LibriSpeech‑960 yields 6.44% WER (small/medium/large) without external LM, first matrix‑MAC‑free spiking network achieving single‑digit WER.
The model also reaches 10.88% test CER on Aishell‑1 (9.28% dev) from scratch, developing a depth‑graded hierarchy of representations.

articles.title: Bio-Inspired Auditory Processing: Coupling Parallel Resonate-and-Fire Dynamics with Ternary Recurrent Networks for Speech Recognition

bullets: MixAgent is an agentic pipeline that emulates audio engineers, grouping tracks, planning effects, and refining mixes guided by a reference song.
A detector identifies needed corrections, and MixCritic—a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques—trains a critic to propose parameter adjustments, reducing mix error by 19%.
Human listening tests show MixAgent outperforms Qwen3‑Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and GPT‑4o‑audio in quality ratings.
Introduces MixAgent, a step‑by‑step system that mimics audio engineers by grouping tracks, planning effects, and creating editable mixing plans using a reference song.
A detector finds problems, and a critic suggests numeric adjustments; trained on 45,657 repair critiques, it is fine‑tuned with preference optimization.
Experiments on MedleyDB show the system reduces mix error by 19% over the initial mix, and human listeners rate it higher than several language models.
MixAgent pipeline: grouping agent routes tracks into subgroups; planning agent selects and orders audio effects (volume, reverb) for tracks, subgroups, full mix.
Refinement: detector flags needed corrections; MixCritic (45,657 critiques) trains critic via supervised learning plus preference optimization, cutting mix error 19% (8.4% more with optimization).
Evaluation: On MedleyDB, MixAgent outperforms Qwen3‑Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT‑4o‑audio in human listening tests, achieving higher quality ratings.

articles.title: Agentic Music Post-Production

bullets: Architecture uses tools and memory to selectively correct wrist PPG heart rate estimates, addressing motion artifacts.

Trained on PPG‑DaLiA and tested on four datasets, the system cut mean absolute error by up to 44.5%, especially on GalaxyPPG, by reducing harmful corrections.
Real‑time prototype on a smartphone lowered error from 9.09 to 4.45 beats per minute in four recordings, showing practical feasibility without extra data rejection.
Agent architecture uses tools and memory around a fixed heart‑rate estimator, generating candidate corrections from pulse, motion, and limited history, then selecting via predicted benefit/harms.
Risk gate retains, corrects, or rejects outputs; trained on PPG‑DaLiA, tested on Wrist Exercise, GalaxyPPG, WildPPG, cutting MAE up to 44.5 %.
Real‑time wearable acquisition, Bluetooth, and smartphone deployment achieved a prototype MAE drop from 9.09 to 4.45 bpm without extra rejection, showing practical feasibility.

bullets: LLMs struggle with classical planning; benchmarks rarely separate structural difficulty from semantic interpretability.
Zero‑training delete‑relaxation heuristic h_add predicts structural difficulty better than learned models (Spearman 0.931 vs 0.707, 0.657, 0.400).
Renaming predicates reduces LLM planning success from 67.5% to 40%; hybrid routing depends on LLM calibration, not just structural scores.
LLMs find classical planning hard, but tests rarely separate structural difficulty (problem layout) from semantic difficulty (symbol meanings).
A zero‑training delete‑relaxation heuristic, h_add, predicts structural difficulty better than learned models like ridge regression or ARC.
Renaming predicates reduces LLM success from 67.5% to 40%, showing semantic changes hurt planning; hybrid systems need better semantic modeling.
Zero‑training delete‑relaxation heuristic h_add predicts structural difficulty with mean Spearman |ρ|=0.931, outperforming ridge regression (0.707), object count (0.657), and ARC (0.400).
Renaming predicates from 0% to 100% drops LLM planning success from 67.5% to 40.0%, while refusals stay at 0%, isolating semantic effects.
Hybrid routing between an LLM and a symbolic planner relies more on calibrating to the target LLM’s outcomes than on the structural score chosen.

articles.title: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability

bullets: Introduces Gradus, a method that treats an environment as a latent syllabus, extracting guarded behavioral operators to guide task creation.
Decouples task objectives from concrete tasks, using corpus-level feedback to target missing outcome combinations and calibrate tasks and solutions against execution feedback.
Demonstrates significant performance gains on benchmarks, boosting 30B model accuracy from 59% to 89% on τ²-Bench and from 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench.
Gradus creates a curriculum that separates learning goals from specific tasks, using the environment itself as a hidden syllabus to generate harder challenges.
It extracts guarded behavioral operators—rules linking actions to conditions and outcomes—and composes them into progressively demanding tasks, guided by feedback that keeps difficult examples.
The approach improves large language models, boosting performance from 59% to 89% on τ²-Bench and 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench, showing effective coverage-guided exploration.

Gradus decouples teaching objectives from concrete tasks, extracting guarded behavioral operators from a fixed environment’s latent syllabus to model action-condition dependencies and effect propagation.
It composes operators into graded tasks, using corpus‑level feedback to target missing outcome combinations while jointly calibrating tasks and solutions via execution feedback.
The curriculum boosts a 30B model from 59%→89% on τ²‑Bench and 47%→83% on CAR‑Bench with an Opus 4.5 proposer, preserving hard examples through recovery‑based verification.

articles.title: GRADUS: Discovering and Recovering Agent Lessons from the Environment's Latent Syllabus

The framework uses a graph‑aware Gaussian Process (a statistical model) and Expected Improvement to rank candidate workflows, offering a clear selection rule versus language‑model guessing.
Experiments on BigCodeBench and TabPFN show evolved MAS outperform systems on code generation and improve preprocessing on time‑series data while staying competitive on standard datasets.
Introduces Bayesian Evolutionary Optimization combining evolutionary operators and graph‑aware Gaussian Process with Expected Improvement to auto‑discover MAS topologies.

bullets: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) embeds adversarial instructions in external data, threatening LLM agents; Attention Tracker detects attacks by monitoring attention between user and data tokens.
Evaluation on AgentDojo shows Attention Tracker's dataset‑agnostic claim fails; long structured tool outputs subvert its assumptions, yielding near‑chance detection across most model families.
AttnDA replaces the scalar threshold with a Fisher Linear Discriminant classifier over per‑head focus scores, improving detection across benchmarks yet struggling to transfer to AgentDojo.
Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is when harmful instructions are hidden in external data that a language model reads, threatening AI agents.
Attention Tracker claims to detect IPI by checking where a model focuses its attention, but tests on AgentDojo show it often fails.
The new AttnDA method replaces a simple threshold with a statistical classifier, improving detection across several tests, though challenges remain.
Attention Tracker monitors attention distribution between user task tokens and data tokens, using a scalar focus score threshold to detect indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks.
Evaluation on AgentDojo shows dataset‑agnostic claim fails; long structured tool outputs subvert assumptions, yielding near‑chance detection across model families.
AttnDA replaces scalar threshold with Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis on per‑head focus vectors, improving detection on multiple benchmarks but still struggling to transfer to AgentDojo.

LEAF is a transformer for FPGAs that uses LUTs (lookup tables) efficiently, achieving nanosecond‑scale inference.
It rewrites attention (focus on important parts) and feed‑forward layers into FPGA‑native forms, tabulating constant matrix‑vector multiplications to reduce resource use.
On jet tagging, it outperforms prior models by 1.8% accuracy, using 2.9× fewer LUTs, achieving 80.4% accuracy at 28k LUTs and 35ns.
LEAF: LUT‑aware Efficient Attention on FPGAs—first nanosecond‑scale transformer converting query/key/value projections and feed‑forward into FPGA‑native layers via LUT‑aware training.
Attention block’s constant matrix‑vector multiplications are tabulated, leaving remaining operations arithmetic, enabling 1.8‑point accuracy gain and 2.9× LUT savings on jet‑tagging benchmark.
Most efficient LEAF‑based linformer with 64 input particles achieves 80.4% accuracy at 28k LUTs and 35 ns latency.

articles.title: LEAF: LUT-aware Efficient Attention on FPGAs

bullets: CovNav uses Conformal Prediction to decide when a fast LLM should trigger slow chain-of-thought reasoning for object navigation tasks.
It treats spatial queries as binary decisions, converting token probabilities into prediction sets and escalating only ambiguous cases.
Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show CovNav outperforms zero‑shot baselines by 0.8–1.7 percentage points.
CovNav uses a fast local LLM to guess if a target object is near another object, then checks uncertainty with Conformal Prediction.
If the prediction is uncertain, CovNav switches to a slow “chain‑of‑thought” mode, trading speed for better reasoning.
Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show CovNav outperforms zero‑shot baselines by up to 1.7 % in success rates.
CovNav uses Conformal Prediction to decide when a fast LLM should defer to slow chain-of-thought reasoning for object goal navigation queries.
The system casts spatial queries as binary decisions, converting token probabilities into prediction sets, and escalates only ambiguous cases, keeping calibration tractable.
Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show CovNav outperforms zero‑shot baselines by 0.8–1.7 pp, supporting open‑set objects via off‑the‑shelf detectors.

articles.title: CovNav: Conformal Prediction-Guided Adaptive Inference for Object Goal Navigation

bullets: Introduces Semantic Observability, a multi‑agent framework that consolidates heterogeneous logs into a dynamic property graph database linking infrastructure, software, and events.
Uses directed cyclic graphs to autonomously traverse the graph, applying causal algorithms and temporal back‑traversal to isolate anomaly blast radii.
An LLM reasoning engine interprets the pruned subgraph to produce code‑level root‑cause analyses and actionable remediations.
Semantic Observability unifies diverse microservice logs into a Property Graph Database, linking infrastructure, software, and events as nodes and directed edges for clearer context.
A multi‑agent system, guided by Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs), automatically traverses the graph, uses causal algorithms and time‑backtracking to pinpoint the exact anomaly area.
The resulting subgraph is fed to a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning engine, which produces code‑level Root Cause Analyses (RCAs) and actionable fixes.

Introduces Semantic Observability: autonomous multi‑agent framework that consolidates heterogeneous microservice logs into a dynamic, queryable Property Graph Database, modeling topology, dependencies, and events.
Employs Directed Cyclic Graphs to orchestrate agents that run causal graph algorithms and temporal back‑traversal, isolating anomaly blast radius within the graph.
Uses an LLM reasoning engine on the pruned subgraph to produce code‑level Root Cause Analyses and actionable remediations, as presented in arXiv:2610.28611v1.

articles.title: Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics

bullets: Introduces RLVR with LLMs for RTL circuit generation from natural language, addressing multi-objective PPA optimization.
Proposes a generation-based training pipeline and Hypervolume Contribution reward to maximize diversity and quality of Pareto-optimal circuit sets.
Demonstrates 13.3% improvement on RTLLM v2 benchmark, indicating superior Pareto front coverage compared to prior single-scalar reward methods.
Uses large language models (LLMs) to write RTL code from natural language, aiming for multiple trade‑offs (power, speed, area) instead of one best design.
Adds a loop that generates circuits sequentially, rewarding each by Hypervolume Contribution (HVC), a metric measuring its improvement to the Pareto front of trade‑offs.
On the RTLLM v2 benchmark, the method boosts the diversity and quality of generated designs by 13.3 % compared to earlier single‑objective RL approaches.
Introduces RLVR with LLMs for RTL circuit generation, addressing multi-objective PPA optimization beyond single scalar rewards.
Proposes generation-based training pipeline converting Pareto coverage into sequential generation, and HVC reward measuring each circuit's contribution to Pareto front.
Evaluated on RTLLM v2 benchmark, achieving +13.3% improvement in reward/diversity over prior methods.

articles.title: Pareto-Optimal RTL Code Generation via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models

bullets: LaLa-World is a language‑conditioned latent world model that learns from simulation, robot data, images, and videos across diverse domains.
It jointly trains a single future predictor using language descriptions of actions and visual changes, built on a language model for interpreting conditions.
The model outperforms domain‑specific LWMs, reduces training cost 6×, speeds planning 13.9×, and initializes LaLa‑Policy, matching Cosmo performance.
LaLa-World is a language‑conditioned latent world model (predicts hidden states) that learns from simulation, robot data, images, and videos.
It uses language to describe actions and visual changes, enabling joint training across diverse datasets.
The model outperforms others in planning, costs less training, plans faster, and can initialize a policy model.
LaLa-World is a language‑conditioned latent world model that jointly learns from simulation, robot trajectories, images, and videos using a single future predictor.
Its predictor, built on a language model, interprets textual action descriptions and visual changes, enabling higher MPC planning performance than domain‑specific LWMs.
Compared to an RAEv2 video baseline, LaLa-World matches planning performance with 6× less training cost and 13.9× faster inference, and pretrains LaLa-Policy for competitive control.

articles.title: LaLa-World: Scaling Latent World Models with Natural Language Actions

bullets: Hybrid framework combining Temporal Fusion Transformer and N-BEATS for multi-horizon PV power forecasting.
Attention-based fusion learns short-term dynamics via TFT and long-term trends via N-BEATS, enabling simultaneous 30‑min to 24‑hr predictions.
Tested on DKASC multi‑year data, outperforms baselines with RMSE reductions up to 3540%.
Hybrid model combines Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) and N-BEATS to capture short‑term and long‑term patterns in PV power.
Attention‑based fusion balances the two branches, producing forecasts for 30‑min to 24‑hr horizons in one pipeline.
Tested on real data from DKASC, the model outperforms baselines, reducing error by up to 3540%.
Hybrid TFT‑N‑BEATS model fuses short‑term TFT and long‑term N‑BEATS via adaptive attention, enabling simultaneous 30‑min to 24‑h PV power forecasts.
TFT captures dynamic feature importance; N‑BEATS decomposes trend/seasonality with interpretable basis functions, improving multi‑scale learning.
On DKASC multi‑year data, the framework reduces RMSE to 42.35–52.29, outperforming baselines by up to 3540 % reduction.

articles.title: A Hybrid TFT-NBEATS Framework for Robust Multi-Horizon Photovoltaic Power Forecasting

bullets: Introduces Continuum-LM, a continuous-depth language model that reuses pretrained residual transformations as dynamical operators, enabling continuous hidden-state evolution.
Uses ordinary differential equations with higher-order numerical integration; solver order and step size control computation, allowing stable training across eight scientific tasks.
Achieves 7.77–10.96% higher exact-match accuracy over discrete counterparts at 0.6B and 1.7B scales, outperforming Ouro-style recurrent control under matched budgets.

Introduces Continuum‑LM, a continuous‑depth (hidden states change continuously) language model that reuses pretrained residual transformations as dynamical operators, evolving via differential equations.
Uses higher-order numerical integration (more accurate calculation of equations), where solver order and step size control computation, enabling flexible depth without adding parameters.
Tested on eight scientific tasks, Continuum‑LM outperforms discrete models by 7.77–10.96% accuracy at 0.6B and 1.7B sizes, showing parameter reuse (same parameters used) boosts performance.

Introduces Continuum‑LM, a continuous‑depth language model that reuses pretrained residual transformations as dynamical operators, evolving hidden states via an ODE solved with higher‑order integration.

bullets: LightCRS is a lightweight framework that unifies multi-domain multimodal conversational recommendation by precomputing product representations and using a small query-conditioned module.
It achieves state‑of‑the‑art HR@1, NDCG@5, and MRR, outperforming baselines by 35.4% HR@1 and reducing latency 266×.

LightCRS is a lightweight system that recommends products across many categories using a single shared model, avoiding separate models for each domain.
It precomputes product images and text with frozen encoders, then uses a 5.3M‑parameter module that fuses queries via cross‑attention and compares candidates with a Transformer.
On a 25‑domain benchmark, LightCRS beats baselines by 35% in top‑1 hits and is 266 times faster per query, while joint training adds 15% accuracy.
LightCRS: lightweight framework using frozen VLM encoders to precompute multimodal product embeddings; online 5.3M-parameter query‑conditioned cross‑attention fuses evidence across domains.
Inter‑candidate Transformer scores candidates; shared across 25 domains, reducing latency 266× and boosting HR@1 by 35.4% over baseline.
MM‑R2A‑25 pairs Reddit dialogues with Amazon listings; joint multi‑domain training improves HR@1 by 15.2% over single‑domain models.

articles.title: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System

bullets: Introduces a prompt-side structural complexity index scoring prompts on six dimensions, avoiding bias from generated code.
Evaluated 5,000 Python prompts with 21 models and four LLM judges; composite ICC(2,1)=0.872 indicates strong inter-rater reliability.
Found a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 14.0 where pass rates jump from 83.4% to 90.1%; breakpoint persists after adjusting for task type.
Introduces a new Prompt‑Side Structural Complexity Index (a score of prompt structure on six dimensions) that avoids bias from broken code.
Tested on 5,000 Python prompts and 21 models; a composite score of 14.0 marks a breakpoint where pass rates rise from 83% to 90%.
Higher prompt complexity can lower failures, but the effect differs by model and source; 25% of failures pair high prompt scores with low output complexity.

articles.title: The Complexity Kink: A Prompt-Side Structural Complexity Index for Code-Generation Reliability

bullets: Harness optimization boosts language model agent performance by better shaping context, tool use, and workflows without updating weights.
The study distinguishes elicitation (improving success on existing tasks) from expansion (enabling new solvable tasks) to guide recursive self‑improvement.
Results show that while optimized harnesses improve pass@1, gains can reverse with larger attempt budgets, and aggregate metrics may mask task‑specific shortfalls.
Harness optimization tweaks context, tool use, and workflows, boosting language‑model agent performance without changing weights.
The study distinguishes “elicitation” (better success on known tasks) from “expansion” (new tasks solved), key for recursive improvement.
Results show gains vary with task difficulty and attempt limits; larger budgets can reduce harness benefits compared to scaling or compute.
Harness optimization shapes context, tool use, and workflows to better leverage LM capabilities without weight updates.
Study distinguishes elicitation (improved success on reachable tasks) vs expansion (broader solvable tasks), using pass@k analysis to compare pre- and post-optimization harnesses.
Findings show pass@1 gains can reverse at higher attempt budgets, and aggregate improvements mask shortfalls on harder tasks, contrasting with model scaling and compute boosts.

articles.title: Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization

bullets: cls fine-tuning outperforms s2s for hallucination detection, creating clear two-cluster geometry and strong class separation.
cls signal saturates before final layer, revealing an InfoWindow where task information emerges; upper layers become redundant.
Removing 31% of layers above InfoWindow keeps accuracy on Qwen3-4B/8B while cutting latency 1.4×.
Fine‑tuning a classifier head (CLS) outperforms a sequence‑to‑sequence (S2S) approach for detecting hallucinations in large language models.
CLS pushes hidden states into two distinct clusters, giving clear class separation and easy linear decoding, while S2S keeps states near the pretrained backbone.
Analysis shows a narrow middle layer window where task information appears; removing upper layers beyond this window cuts latency 1.4× without losing accuracy.
Classifier‑head fine‑tuning (cls) outperforms seq‑to‑seq (s2s) on binary hallucination detection by inducing a two‑cluster geometry with strong class separation and linearly decodable labels.
Cls signal saturates before the final layer, creating an upper‑middle InfoWindow where task information emerges, followed by a redundant upper plateau that mirrors this signal.
Removing layers above the InfoWindow truncates 31% of Qwen3‑4B/8B, preserving accuracy within seed noise while cutting latency by 1.4×.

articles.title: How Fine-Tuning Objectives Shape Layer-Wise Information in LLM Hallucination Detection

bullets: LatticeMind transforms natural-language requests into validated DFT workflows, using contracts and deterministic pre-execution checks to ensure correct stages, files, and dependencies before solver runs.
On a 44-case RESCU benchmark, 119/132 runs succeeded on first plan, with remaining completed after one repair; ablation shows contracts and validation are key.

LatticeMind turns natural language into DFT workflows, ensuring each step’s files and dependencies are correct before running the solver. Define DFT: quantum simulation of electrons.
It uses a workflow contract and validators to catch errors early; if a check fails, a limited repair is attempted, keeping results traceable.
Tested on 44 RESCU and 19 VASP cases, it matched all reference results, outperforming a simple trial‑and‑repair approach with fewer tokens.
LatticeMind converts natural‑language requests into executable DFT projects via a workflow contract, deterministic validators, and bounded repair before solver launch.
On a 44‑case RESCU benchmark, 119/132 runs succeeded on first validated plan, with remaining passing after one repair cycle.
Ablation studies show workflow contract and pre‑execution validation are key, while the framework reproduces all reference values on a 19‑case VASP benchmark, proving solver transferability.

articles.title: LatticeMind: A Validation-Gated Agentic Framework for Density Functional Theory Workflows

bullets: Study of ordered layer-state trajectories in transformers shows layer order significantly shapes inference, aligning 1.6–2.2× more with endpoint than shuffled order.

Hidden-state coordinates outperform vocabulary readbacks; architecture-specific scaffolds identified across Qwen, Llama, Gemma, with interventions controlling trajectories via local actuators and gating.
Selective gating achieved 17/87 Qwen closure trajectories to top‑1 boundary, demonstrating behaviorally consequential process without fine‑grained dose assignment.
The study examines how the sequence of transformer layers (layer-state trajectory: hidden states across layers) shapes the model’s computation during inference.
Across Qwen, Llama, Gemma, natural layer order aligns 1.6–2.2× better with final outputs than shuffled orders, highlighting architecture over training.
Interventions on hidden states and selective gating can steer internal trajectories, improving specific outputs while leaving others unchanged, demonstrating controllable inference dynamics.
Layer-state trajectories in Qwen, Llama, Gemma show 1.60–2.24× better alignment with endpoint chords than shuffled orders, revealing architecture‑compatible scaffolds across random initializations.

Hidden‑state coordinates outperform vocabulary readbacks; task‑defined coordinates enable computable candidate competition, while additive interventions fail but local transition actuators selectively steer trajectories.
A confidence gate and safety‑matched action reassignment selectively gate 17/87 Qwen closure paths to top‑1 boundaries, demonstrating bounded actuator families without fine‑grained dose control.

articles.title: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference

bullets: Introduces a self-consistency framework that uses diffusion-sampled reasoning trajectories and a reward model to score intermediate steps.
The framework stitches top-scoring steps across trajectories into a composite rationale, then recomputes the final answer, separating exploration from evaluation.
Applied to math and coding benchmarks, the method boosts accuracy up to 23.8% without training, especially on harder problems.
The paper introduces a method that uses diffusion language models to generate many short reasoning steps, then picks the best ones.
Each step is scored by a reward model, and the top steps from different runs are stitched together to form a new, stronger explanation.
The stitched explanation is used to recompute the final answer, boosting accuracy on math and coding tasks by up to 23.8% without extra training.
Diffusion LM samples many low‑cost reasoning chains; each intermediate step is scored by a process reward model (PRM).
Highest‑scoring steps from different trajectories are stitched into a composite rationale, then a final solver recomputes the answer.
Training‑free, reward‑guided stitching boosts accuracy up to 23.8% on six math and coding benchmarks, especially on harder problems.

articles.title: Test-Time Scaling with Diffusion Language Models via Reward-Guided Stitching

bullets: AOI is a multi‑agent framework that turns failed operational trajectories into training signals for autonomous cloud diagnosis.
It employs GRPO for preference‑based learning, a read‑write separated execution architecture, and a closed‑loop evolver to mine failures.
On the AIOpsLab benchmark, AOI reaches 66.3% best@5 success, outpacing the prior 41.9% by 24.4 points.
AOI is a multi‑agent system that turns failed operations into learning signals for autonomous cloud diagnosis, improving reliability without exposing sensitive data.
It uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), tweaking actions based on group performance, to teach models, observation, reasoning, and action to keep environments safe.
On the AIOpsLab benchmark, AOI reaches 66.3% success on 86 tasks, beating previous best (41.9%) by 24.4 points.
AOI: multi‑agent framework turning operations into trajectory learning under security constraints, using GRPO‑based diagnostic models for preference‑based learning without sensitive data exposure.
Read‑write separated execution splits observation, reasoning, action phases, enabling safe learning while preventing unauthorized state mutation in permission‑governed environments.
Failure Trajectory Closed‑Loop Evolver mines unsuccessful paths, converting them into corrective supervision, boosting AOI runtime to 66.3% best@5 on 86 tasks (vs 41.9% prior).

bullets: Agentic AI enables cloud workflows where autonomous agents reason, invoke tools, modify infra, deploy services, verify outcomes, adapt over long tasks.

Framework separates graph engineering (workflow progression & verification), loop engineering (diagnosis, repair, retry), and agent harness engineering (zero-trust execution via identity, policy, isolation).
Evaluation on Google Cloud shows validated code repos, controlled execution, evidence-gated progression, operational deployment, and bounded recovery.
Agentic AI lets autonomous agents manage cloud tasks, from planning to deployment, by reasoning about state and using authorized tools.
The framework splits work into graph engineering (workflow steps and checks), loop engineering (bounded fixes and retries), and agent harness (zero‑trust security).
Tested on Google Cloud, it shows complete code repos, safe execution, evidence‑based progress, and limited recovery within set limits.
Graph engineering defines long‑horizon workflow progression and verification‑dependent transitions, enabling machine‑checkable repository and deployment evidence.
Loop engineering supplies bounded diagnosis, repair, re‑planning, retry, and re‑verification, constraining failure recovery within explicit operational bounds and termination criteria.

Agent harness engineering enforces zero‑trust execution via identity, authorization, policy‑scoped capabilities, isolation, and runtime safeguards, validated on Google Cloud with evidence‑gated progression.

articles.title: Towards Agentic Cloud Engineering: Graph and Loop Engineering with a Zero-Trust Agent Harness

bullets: Difflet is a serving engine for diffusion transformer models on AWS Trainium, sharing a single compilation backend across five pipelines.
It splits attention across cores by head, uses a host controller to decide per denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse cached output.
Across five image and video families, fused attention speeds denoiser steps 1.2–4.3× over PyTorch/XLA, and resident serving is 1.5–3.4× faster than reloading weights.
Difflet is a fast inference engine for diffusion transformer models on AWS Trainium, sharing a single compilation backend across five pipelines.
It splits joint attention across cores by head, and a host controller decides each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse earlier output.
The system speeds up denoiser steps 1.2–4.3× over PyTorch/XLA and makes resident serving 1.5–3.4× faster than reloading weights for each generation.
Difflet compiles all diffusion components ahead of time on AWS Trainium2, sharing a single backend across five pipelines, splitting joint attention by head across cores.
A host controller and device‑side probe decide per denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse cached output, keeping programs resident across requests.
Fused attention yields 1.2–4.3× speedups over PyTorch/XLA, enabling 32.8k‑token attention compilation and 1.5–3.4× faster resident serving versus weight‑reload runs.

articles.title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium

bullets: SPLIT allocates test-time compute among sampling, model choice, and verification using a pilot dataset and an exact probability formula.
The method accounts for task difficulty, shared blind spots, and verifier correlations, fitting parameters via empirical Bayes.

SPLIT uses a small pilot set to decide how many model outputs to generate and how much compute to spend on checking them, boosting accuracy.
It calculates the chance of a correct answer by modeling accept/reject and top‑score selection, accounting for task difficulty, shared blind spots, and correlated verifier errors.
Across 7 benchmarks and 175 agent systems, SPLIT outperforms rule‑of‑thumb budgets, staying within 0.8% of the best hindsight allocation, while fixed rules lose ≥2.5%.
SPLIT uses an accept/reject & top‑score probability formula, fitted via empirical Bayes on a labeled pilot to allocate compute among sampling, mixing, and verification.
It models task difficulty, shared blind spots, and correlated verifier calls, enabling budget planning across 7 benchmarks, 26 models, 175 agents, and 6 verifiers.
In experiments, SPLIT achieves within 0.02–0.8 pp of hindsight‑optimal allocation, outperforming rule‑of‑thumb baselines that lose ≥2.5 pp in some settings.

articles.title: Sample, Mix, or Verify? Allocating Test-Time Compute under Imperfect Verifiers

LoongSage: 14K‑line, fully asynchronous RL framework built on Megatron and SGLang, centralizing orchestration in one controller and using Ray actors for GPU components.

bullets: TP constrain transformer architecture to extract readable Python code, revealing learned computations beyond token accuracy.
